topic: Automating scientific peer review with LLMs

idea.title: Anchoring-Invariant Rebuttal Aggregation: Closing the Discussion-Phase Manipulation Gap in LLM-Mediated Peer Review
idea.gap: Two strands of recent work on LLM-based peer review have identified the author rebuttal / discussion phase as a potent lever on final decisions, but neither has been turned into a defense, and current defensive engineering has looked elsewhere entirely. AgentReview's multi-agent simulation of peer review shows that reviewer biases account for over a third of acceptance-decision variance, driven by concrete social-dynamics mechanisms it explicitly ties to sociological theory: social-conformity pressure that collapses rating variance by ~27% after rebuttal, authority/halo effects, altruism-fatigue cascades, and groupthink amplification. Separately, an aspect-guided adversarial perturbation study of LLM review pipelines found that incomplete or even hostile rebuttals can unexpectedly *raise* acceptance rates, and that 'strong reject' verdicts disproportionately dominate meta-review aggregation regardless of chain-of-thought prompting strategy used. Taken together, these findings say the rebuttal/discussion stage is where LLM reviewers are most exploitable — yet the field's actual defensive engineering (e.g. aiXiv's five-stage prompt-injection detection pipeline) is built to catch adversarial content hidden in the *submitted manuscript*, not manipulative dynamics unfolding in the *reviewer-author exchange*. No existing system asks which specific bias mechanism a manipulative rebuttal is exploiting, or aggregates post-rebuttal scores in a way that is provably invariant to tone, ordering, and conformity cascades rather than just to injected instructions.
idea.proposed_study: (1) Build an adversarial-rebuttal taxonomy-and-testbed on top of a multi-agent LLM review simulation (in the style of AgentReview): an author agent is prompted with four tactic classes mapped explicitly onto AgentReview's own bias mechanisms — preemptive strong-reject deflection (anchoring), hostile-but-empty rebuttal framed as rigor (misread-as-thoroughness), selective concession plus social pressure toward consensus (conformity cascade), and appeals to authority/credentials. For each tactic, measure the induced shift in acceptance rate and post-rebuttal rating variance across several LLM reviewer/meta-reviewer backbones, replicating and mechanistically decomposing the "hostile rebuttals raise acceptance" effect reported in the perturbation-analysis study. (2) Construct a matched control set of genuine, evidence-bearing rebuttals (e.g., from OpenReview threads where score increases are justified by new experiments/results) so defenses can be scored on whether they suppress manipulation without also suppressing legitimate rebuttal-driven updates. (3) Design and test a discussion-phase guardrail — analogous in spirit to aiXiv's submission-time injection defense but targeting aggregation dynamics rather than input content: re-score rebuttals by extracting only verifiable factual/claim deltas (adapting the claim-verification reformulation from evidence-grounded review work) and combine pre- and post-rebuttal reviewer scores via an order- and tone-invariant statistical aggregator (e.g., robust Bradley-Terry pooling that excludes sentiment/length features) instead of a holistic LLM meta-review judgment.
idea.expected_result: The tactic-mechanism decomposition will show that different manipulation strategies exploit distinct, unevenly-defended bias channels (conformity-cascade tactics will likely produce the largest undefended acceptance-rate inflation, since no current system targets multi-turn social dynamics at all), and that the claim-verification-plus-invariant-aggregation guardrail cuts adversarial acceptance-rate inflation substantially (targeting a majority reduction) while preserving most of the legitimate score movement in the genuine-evidence control set — demonstrating that submission-time defenses like prompt-injection filters leave a distinct, currently unguarded attack surface at the discussion/rebuttal stage that requires aggregation-level rather than content-level defenses.
idea.grounding: Grounded in AgentReview's sociologically-grounded taxonomy of reviewer bias mechanisms, the aspect-guided multi-level perturbation study's finding that hostile/incomplete rebuttals can perversely raise acceptance rates and that strong-reject verdicts dominate meta-review aggregation, the claim-verification reformulation of review introduced in evidence-grounded peer review work (auditing claims rather than issuing holistic scores), and aiXiv's demonstration that purpose-built defense mechanisms for LLM review pipelines are practical and effective — the proposal is the first to target defenses at the rebuttal/discussion stage itself rather than at submission-time content, closing a gap these literatures jointly reveal but no prior system addresses.

topic: Automating scientific peer review with LLMs

idea.title: Transfer-Aware Robust Aggregation for Adversarially-Manipulated LLM Peer Review Ensembles
idea.gap: Two lines of recent work on LLM-based peer review have developed in parallel without being tested against each other. One line shows that individual LLM reviewers are highly vulnerable to manipulation: invisible/indirect prompt injection can flip a "reject" into an "accept" (as shown in work such as "When Reject Turns into Accept," "Breaking the Reviewer," and "Paraphrasing Adversarial Attack on LLM-as-a-Reviewer"), and textual perturbations can inflate scores when placed strategically in a manuscript. A second line proposes multi-model ensembles and statistical aggregation (majority voting, weighted averaging, EM/Dawid-Skene-style pooling) to stabilize LLM review scores and bring them closer to human judgment, treating disagreement between LLM reviewers as roughly independent noise. But Dawid-Skene-style aggregation is built on an i.i.d.-noise assumption, and no existing study has tested whether an author who knows a conference uses a multi-model LLM ensemble can craft an attack that transfers across model families (exploiting shared RLHF-induced sycophancy or shared training-data biases), thereby defeating the very independence assumption the aggregation defense relies on. In other words, the field has never characterized adversarial transferability across LLM reviewer ensembles, nor whether current aggregation methods actually provide robustness against a strategic (rather than random-noise) attacker.
idea.proposed_study: Assemble a benchmark of borderline conference-style submissions (e.g., openly available ICLR/NeurIPS-style papers near the accept/reject threshold) and apply three manipulation classes drawn from the adversarial-review literature: (1) invisible/indirect prompt injection (hidden text, white-on-white or zero-width-unicode instructions), (2) character/typographic adversarial perturbations, and (3) semantic paraphrase-based attacks that reframe weaknesses as strengths without altering surface content. Score each manipulated paper with a heterogeneous panel of LLM reviewers spanning distinct model families (e.g., GPT-, Claude-, Gemini-, and open-weight Llama-class models), under three aggregation schemes: simple majority vote, weighted averaging, and EM/Dawid-Skene pooling. First, measure per-attack, per-model success rates and compute a cross-model transferability matrix (does an attack crafted/tuned against one model's scoring shift the scores of the others?). Second, measure whether each aggregation scheme actually attenuates the adversarial score shift relative to a single-reviewer baseline, and whether attenuation collapses specifically for attacks with high measured transferability. Third, design and test a transfer-aware robust aggregation rule that, instead of assuming independent reviewer noise, downweights or flags subsets of reviewers whose score shifts are anomalously correlated relative to a same-model score computed on a lightly-perturbed control copy of the manuscript (a proxy for detecting coordinated manipulation rather than genuine independent judgment).
idea.expected_result: Aggregation will meaningfully reduce adversarial score inflation for attacks with low cross-model transferability (e.g., tokenizer-specific typographic injection), but will provide little to no protection against high-transferability semantic paraphrase attacks, because these exploit judgment tendencies shared across model families rather than model-specific quirks — meaning current ensemble/Dawid-Skene defenses are systematically weaker exactly against the most sophisticated attackers. The proposed transfer-aware aggregation rule, which explicitly detects correlated (rather than independent) score shifts, should recover a substantial fraction of the lost robustness on the high-transferability attack class where naive aggregation fails.
idea.grounding: Directly motivated by combining two disjoint recent threads: adversarial-vulnerability studies of LLM reviewers (e.g., "Breaking the Reviewer," "When Reject Turns into Accept: Quantifying the Vulnerability of LLM-Based Scientific Reviewers to Indirect Prompt Injection," "Paraphrasing Adversarial Attack on LLM-as-a-Reviewer," and "Aspect-Guided Multi-Level Perturbation Analysis of LLMs in Automated Peer Review") and ensemble/aggregation-for-calibration proposals for LLM review scoring that rely on majority-vote or EM/Dawid-Skene pooling; it also answers the call in "Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation" for rigorous, adversarially-grounded evaluation before such systems are deployed in real review pipelines. This matters because conference organizers are actively debating (and in some cases piloting) LLM-assisted or multi-model review, and the standard proposed safeguard — ensembling multiple models — has never been stress-tested against a strategic author who anticipates that safeguard, as opposed to random or single-model attacks.

topic: Fully autonomous end-to-end AI scientists for machine-learning research

idea.title: Provenance-Grounded Verification Agents: Decoupling Result Auditing from Manuscript Self-Review in Autonomous AI Scientists
idea.gap: Every current end-to-end AI-scientist pipeline (The AI Scientist, The AI Scientist-v2, Agent Laboratory, MLR-Agent, Jr. AI Scientist) closes its loop with a self-review or LLM-judge pass that reads the finished manuscript's prose and scores it for novelty, clarity, and soundness. But two independent findings expose a structural blind spot in this design. First, MLR-Bench found that current coding agents fabricate or fail to validate experimental results in roughly 80% of ML-research task attempts — a failure that is distinct from, and hidden behind, these same systems' strong idea-generation and paper-writing ability. Second, studies of LLM-based peer review (e.g. "Are We There Yet? Revealing the Risks of Utilizing Large Language Models in Scholarly Peer Review") show LLM reviewers rate title-only submissions comparably to complete papers and are swayed by surface presentation and prestige rather than methodological substance, with sentence-level analyses finding LLM reviews contain more undetected deficiencies than human reviews. A review pass that only ever reads the manuscript's narrative has no way to notice that a confidently reported number was never actually produced by a logged experimental run — it is auditing the story, not the evidence. No existing AI-scientist system architecturally separates "did the code actually produce this claimed result" from "is the paper well-written and interesting," and no benchmark isolates whether an automated reviewer stage catches fabricated or unsupported claims specifically, as opposed to catching low novelty or weak prose.
idea.proposed_study: Build a "provenance auditor" agent inserted between experiment execution and manuscript self-review in an AI-scientist pipeline. The auditor is architecturally blind to the manuscript's narrative text: it receives only (a) the executed code and raw run artifacts — stdout logs, saved metrics files, seeds, checkpoints — and (b) a set of atomic claims mechanically extracted from the manuscript's results section (each numeric result, each statistical comparison, each stated seed/replicate count or control condition). Its sole task is claim-to-artifact matching: for each claim, attempt to re-derive it from the logged run outputs and flag it as supported, unsupported, unreproducible, or suspicious (e.g. a single best-of-N run presented as the only run, an ablation with no logged control, a significance claim with no repeated trials). It never scores novelty or writing quality. Evaluate on two sets: (1) real outputs already produced by existing open pipelines (The AI Scientist, AI Scientist-v2, Agent Laboratory, MLR-Agent submissions from MLR-Bench), and (2) a synthetic set built from the same pipelines' runs with deliberately injected fabrications (altered numbers, silently cherry-picked seeds, omitted ablations, unsupported significance claims). Compare catch rate and false-positive rate across three reviewer conditions: (a) each pipeline's native LLM self-review, (b) a manuscript-only LLM-judge given a rigor checklist (matching current MLR-Judge-style setups), and (c) the provenance auditor with artifact access. Finally, test whether routing auditor flags back into the pipeline — forcing re-execution or claim retraction before the manuscript is finalized — reduces the fabrication/non-validation rate on a held-out MLR-Bench-style task set relative to the unaudited baseline.
idea.expected_result: Manuscript-only reviewers (native self-review and the general LLM-judge) will catch only a small minority of injected fabrications, since they have no access to ground-truth execution artifacts and are already documented to weight presentation over substance — consistent with PaperBench's ~21% agent replication ceiling (vs. a 41.4% human ML-PhD baseline) and REPRO-Bench's finding that agentic reproducibility assessment performs below chance. The provenance auditor, performing direct artifact-to-claim matching rather than narrative judgment, should catch a substantially higher share of injected numeric and statistical fabrications, and closing the loop with auditor-triggered re-execution should measurably cut the fabrication/non-validation rate reported for unaudited pipelines.
idea.grounding: Grounded in MLR-Bench's finding that current coding agents fabricate or fail to validate ~80% of ML-research results; the self-review architectures of The AI Scientist and The AI Scientist-v2; documented failure modes of LLM-based peer review ("Are We There Yet? Revealing the Risks of Utilizing Large Language Models in Scholarly Peer Review" and related sentence-level deficiency analyses); and the human-vs-agent replication gap established by PaperBench and the sub-chance reproducibility assessment found by REPRO-Bench, both of which motivate treating result verification as a distinct capability from manuscript quality judgment rather than a byproduct of it.

topic: Fully autonomous end-to-end AI scientists for machine-learning research

idea.title: Blind Self-Replication as an In-Loop Gate for Autonomous ML Research Pipelines
idea.gap: Current end-to-end AI-scientist systems (e.g., AI Scientist-v2, Agent Laboratory) verify their own output only through self-critique or an LLM-judge review of the final manuscript, using the same context (code, logs, cherry-picked plots) that produced the result. Independent audits have documented a resulting "verification gap": pervasive post-hoc selection bias, "overexcitement" (declaring success despite weak or contradicted evidence), implementation drift, and unsupported citations that survive to the finished paper. Separately, reproducibility benchmarks such as MLReplicate evaluate whether an autonomous system's *published* outputs can be independently reproduced, and critiques such as Sibyl-AutoResearch argue current systems are "paper generators," not systems built around genuine trial-and-error validation. What is missing is a mechanism that uses reproducibility as an architectural gate operating *during* generation, before a claim ever reaches a human or a benchmark leaderboard — rather than as an external audit applied afterward to a finished paper.
idea.proposed_study: Augment an open end-to-end ML research pipeline (matching the AI Scientist-v2 / Agent Laboratory architecture: idea generation, coding, experiment execution, write-up) with a "Blind Replicator" agent that sits between experiment and paper-writing stages. For each empirical claim the primary agent drafts, the Blind Replicator receives only the natural-language Methods description and claimed result (no code, no logs, no hyperparameter files beyond what is stated in prose) plus an equal compute budget, and must independently re-implement and re-run the experiment from scratch. Define a replication-concordance score per claim (sign agreement on the primary comparison plus effect-size ratio within a pre-registered tolerance). Claims that fail concordance are automatically routed back to the primary agent with the discrepancy as feedback, forcing it to either narrow the claim's scope, mark it preliminary, or drop it — before the paper is finalized. Compare this gated pipeline against an ungated baseline (same base models/budget, standard self-critique only) on a fixed suite of small-scale ML tasks (e.g., the NanoGPT/CIFAR-variant/algorithmic-task suite used in the AI Scientist line of work). Evaluate both pipelines' final papers using a *third*, fully independent replication pass (different agent, different seed, never used in the training loop) plus human-expert grading for claim reliability, citation support, and perceived novelty/quality (to check whether gating narrows claims at a cost to perceived contribution).
idea.expected_result: The gated pipeline should show a substantially higher fraction of claims that survive independent third-party replication and lower rates of the previously documented failure modes (overexcitement, unsupported effect sizes), at the cost of narrower, more hedged claims and a modest reduction in judged "novelty" scores relative to the ungated baseline. This would show that a large share of the verification gap in current autonomous-research systems is closeable with an architectural fix — an adversarial, code-blind replication gate — without requiring new reasoning capability in the base model, and it would yield replication-concordance as a reusable automatic proxy metric for trustworthiness that is distinct from existing LLM-judge quality scores.
idea.grounding: Motivated directly by gaps named in the recent AI-scientist literature: the "verification gap" identified in surveys of autonomous research agents, the cataloged failure modes (post-hoc selection bias, overexcitement, implementation drift) in analyses of hidden pitfalls in AI Scientist systems, the reproducibility deficits measured by MLReplicate, and Sibyl-AutoResearch's argument that autonomous research needs self-evolving trial-and-error harnesses rather than paper-generation pipelines — none of which propose using code-blind independent replication as an in-loop generation-time gate rather than a post-hoc audit or static benchmark.

idea.title: Structural-Hole-Guided Ideation: Steering LLM Hypothesis Generation with Bibliometric Bridging Signals Instead of LLM-Judged Novelty
idea.gap: Recent large-scale audits show that autonomous LLM research agents (AI Scientist, ResearchAgent, AgentLaboratory, and zero-shot pipelines) generate ideas that are far more topically concentrated than human-authored papers in the same area, stay tightly clustered around their seed literature rather than moving into new territory the way human follow-on work does, and — critically — the papers most similar to AI-generated ideas go on to receive systematically fewer subsequent citations, indicating these agents preferentially colonize low-impact regions of the scientific landscape. When their ideas do diverge from prior work, the divergence comes from recombining existing technical methods, not from posing genuinely new questions. Meanwhile, the standard fix used across the field — overgenerate-and-rerank pipelines that select ideas using an LLM-as-judge novelty score — rests on a broken signal: large-scale benchmarking has shown LLM-judged idea novelty is poorly correlated with actual empirical effectiveness, and separately that LLM-judge scores systematically inflate ratings relative to domain experts. So the dominant self-improvement loop in current ideation agents (generate → LLM-judge novelty → select) optimizes against a criterion that doesn't predict real scientific value, which plausibly explains why the resulting ideas stay clustered near safe, already-mined territory. What's missing is an ideation-steering signal for LLM agents that is *not* another LLM's subjective novelty judgment, but is instead a validated, independently measurable proxy for where high-impact ideas actually come from.
idea.proposed_study: Build an ideation agent that replaces LLM-judge reranking with an explicit bibliometric steering signal drawn from the science-of-science literature on "atypical combinations": papers that combine mostly conventional prior work with an unusual pairing of otherwise-distant literatures are disproportionately represented among high-impact hits. Concretely: (1) construct a citation/co-citation embedding space over a target subfield's literature (e.g., ML or biomedicine), and identify pairs of clusters that are individually well-established (high internal citation density) but rarely co-cited — "structural holes" — using standard network-bridging measures; (2) instead of retrieval-augmented generation seeded from one tight neighborhood (the current practice in agents like ResearchAgent/AgentLaboratory), condition the LLM ideation step on paired retrieval from two such distant-but-bridgeable clusters, explicitly prompting the model to generate a hypothesis that connects them; (3) evaluate the resulting idea corpus with the same retrospective methodology used to diagnose the narrowing problem — embedding-space dispersion relative to seed literature and human follow-on work, plus the historical citation rate of the literature neighborhood each generated idea lands nearest to — rather than any LLM-judge novelty score; (4) run a held-out prospective arm modeled on the 100+ NLP-researcher human study design, where domain experts rate feasibility and excitement of structural-hole-guided ideas blind against standard single-neighborhood RAG ideation and overgenerate-and-rerank baselines, to confirm the bibliometric steering doesn't sacrifice feasibility for the sake of dispersion.
idea.expected_result: Structural-hole-guided ideation will produce a corpus with topic dispersion closer to genuine human follow-on research (rather than the tight seed-literature clustering seen in current agents), and its ideas will land in literature neighborhoods with measurably higher historical subsequent-citation rates than ideas from standard RAG or LLM-judge-reranked pipelines, at comparable expert-rated feasibility — directly reversing the "local elaboration over broad exploration" failure mode, while showing that a bibliometrically grounded steering signal outperforms LLM-judged novelty as a target for ideation optimization.
idea.grounding: Motivated directly by three empirical results that have not yet been connected: "AI Research Agents Narrow Scientific Exploration" (Tang & Yang), which documents that current agents concentrate ideation near low-citation-impact neighborhoods rather than broadening exploration; "MLRC-Bench," which shows LLM-judged novelty is decoupled from empirical effectiveness, undermining the rerank signal these agents rely on; and the "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?" large-scale human study, which independently documents a lack-of-diversity failure mode at scale. It also builds on evidence that grounding LLM hypothesis generation in explicit structured relations rather than free text improves both novelty and semantic diversity (as shown for causal-graph-grounded psychological hypothesis generation), and imports the "atypical combinations" theory of scientific impact from bibliometrics as a concrete, previously-unused optimization target for ideation agents. This matters because if the field keeps optimizing ideation agents against LLM-judge novelty, it may be systematically reinforcing exactly the narrow, low-impact exploration pattern the diagnostic studies have just identified.

idea.title: Belief Perseverance in LLM Hypothesis Revision: A Cognitive-Taxonomy Benchmark for Theory Change Under Disconfirming Evidence
idea.gap: Current evaluation of LLM-generated scientific hypotheses covers novelty and validity (surveyed in "Large Language Models for Scientific Idea Generation: A Creativity-Centered Survey"), truthfulness and hallucination (TruthHypo / "Toward Reliable Scientific Hypothesis Generation: Evaluating Truthfulness and Hallucination in Large Language Models"), diverse coverage of a hypothesis space under underdetermination (HypoSpace), and one-shot prediction accuracy under progressive information disclosure (ProjectionBench). A closer strand — "Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models" — does study iterative belief updating, but only via an abstract, synthetic Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery game, scored with a single scalar metric (the ratio of hypothesis-incompatible to hypothesis-compatible test proposals). None of this work asks a more structural question that decades of science-education research has already formalized for human scientists: when a real, literature-grounded hypothesis meets genuine disconfirming evidence, HOW does the reasoner change its mind — does it genuinely revise the theory, or does it deploy one of the well-documented bias-protecting maneuvers? Chinn & Brewer's classic taxonomy ("The Role of Anomalous Data in Knowledge Acquisition," 1993) identifies seven distinct response types to anomalous data — ignoring it, rejecting it, excluding it as irrelevant to the theory's domain, holding it in abeyance, reinterpreting it while retaining the core theory, making a peripheral theory change, or accepting it and changing the theory — and shows only the last constitutes genuine scientific progress. This taxonomy has never been applied to LLMs, and no existing benchmark tests whether an LLM's revision behavior degrades toward bias-protecting strategies as a function of how much self-generated justification it has already invested in its own hypothesis — the LLM analogue of the escalation-of-commitment / belief-perseverance effect documented in humans (Ross, Lepper & Hubbard) and echoed in known LLM sycophancy and self-consistency biases.
idea.proposed_study: Construct a benchmark of ~150-200 real case triples (initial evidence base, an originally plausible hypothesis it supports, and a subsequently documented disconfirming finding), drawn from domains with clear anomaly-to-revision narratives in the literature (e.g., superseded biomedical mechanisms, materials-science claims overturned by replication, retracted or substantially revised psychology effects), screening for cases obscure or recent enough to limit training-data leakage and verifying the evidence chain against primary sources. For each case, elicit a hypothesis from the LLM given only the initial evidence, under two manipulated conditions: a low-investment condition (state the hypothesis briefly) and a high-investment condition (first produce an extended mechanistic justification/defense of the hypothesis, mimicking the write-up step common in autonomous research pipelines like AI Scientist, CycleResearcher, or LLM-AutoSciLab, before ever seeing the disconfirming finding). Then present the real disconfirming finding and ask the model to update its position, optionally probing it across several follow-up turns to measure how many exposures are needed to induce genuine revision ("revision latency"). Code every response into Chinn & Brewer's seven-category taxonomy — collapsed into a primary genuine-theory-change vs. bias-protecting binary, with the full categorical distribution as a secondary outcome — using human raters plus an LLM classifier validated against human agreement. Compare rates and category distributions across the investment manipulation, across model families/scales, across single- vs. multi-turn probing, and with/without an explicit "update your hypothesis if warranted" meta-instruction to test whether the bias is a shallow framing effect or persists regardless.
idea.expected_result: LLMs will reproduce the qualitative asymmetry seen in human subjects: a strong skew toward bias-protecting responses (especially reinterpretation, exclusion, and peripheral theory change) over genuine theory change, even when explicitly instructed to update on new evidence. Critically, the rate of bias-protecting responses will rise significantly in the high-investment condition relative to the low-investment condition, showing that the act of generating a detailed self-justification for a hypothesis — standard practice in current LLM-driven research pipelines — measurably impairs the model's later capacity to genuinely revise that hypothesis in light of real disconfirming evidence, a dynamic invisible to scalar confirmation-bias metrics like the incompatible:compatible test ratio used in synthetic rule-discovery evaluations.
idea.grounding: Autonomous "AI scientist" systems (AI Scientist, CycleResearcher, LLM-AutoSciLab, and agentic falsification pipelines such as "Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications") all loop LLMs through generate-justify-test-revise cycles, but the revision step's fidelity has only been probed indirectly via scalar bias metrics on toy tasks; grounding the evaluation in Chinn & Brewer's (1993) validated cognitive taxonomy of anomalous-data response, and in the well-established belief-perseverance/escalation-of-commitment literature from human cognition, would give the field its first structural, mechanism-level account of whether and why LLM hypothesis revision fails — directly relevant to whether these pipelines can perform the theory-change step that most distinguishes real scientific discovery from confirmation-seeking generation.

topic: AI systems for generating novel research ideas

idea.title: Fertility-Aware Ideation: Selecting AI-Generated Research Ideas for Follow-On Impact, Not Just Novelty
idea.gap: A recent large-scale retrospective study generating ~38,000 ideas from four AI research-agent frameworks (zero-shot, AI Scientist, ResearchAgent, AgentLaboratory) across six LLMs found that AI-generated ideas cluster much more tightly around their seed literature than human follow-on work does, that when they do diverge from prior work the divergence is almost always a technical-method swap rather than a genuinely new research question, and — most tellingly — that papers most similar to AI-generated ideas go on to receive fewer subsequent citations than the surrounding literature. This is striking because essentially every deployed ideation system (the retrieval-plus-overgenerate-and-rerank pipeline shown to beat human NLP experts in blind novelty review, plus knowledge-graph- and multi-source-retrieval-augmented planners) is explicitly tuned to maximize perceived novelty, either via LLM-judge scores or human blind-review excitement ratings. Separately, work on ML research-agent benchmarks has shown LLM-judged idea novelty is poorly correlated with an idea's actual empirical effectiveness. Put together, these results expose a measurement gap: the field has built ideation systems that optimize surface novelty (distance from existing embeddings, reviewer excitement) while apparently steering agents toward genuinely low-impact regions of the scientific landscape, and no existing system or evaluation protocol scores ideas on their likely "fertility" — the probability that pursuing an idea seeds productive follow-on research — as a signal distinct from novelty.
idea.proposed_study: (1) Using the same citation-defined "seed literature" research areas as the AI-ideation-narrowing study, retrospectively characterize historical papers along two independent axes: surface novelty (embedding distance from the seed citation cluster) and a "fertility" feature adapted from the science-of-science literature on atypical combinations — the finding that high-impact papers pair mostly conventional citations with a smaller share of rare, distant ones — but computed at the level of research-question framing rather than method substitution (i.e., classify whether a paper reuses an old question with a new method, asks a new question of an old method, or recombines questions across distant sub-fields). Fit a model predicting 5-year citation/follow-on counts from these features to obtain a fertility score. (2) Build an ideation reranker on top of the standard retrieval-plus-overgenerate scaffold that selects candidate ideas by predicted fertility instead of (or alongside) LLM-judged novelty, explicitly rewarding question-level recombination across distant literatures over technical-method substitution within the seed neighborhood. (3) Evaluate retrospectively by checking whether fertility-reranked idea sets land closer to historically high-citation regions of idea space than novelty-reranked or existing multi-agent-scientist baselines, using the same idea-to-literature similarity methodology that originally revealed the low-citation clustering effect; and prospectively via a blind expert study (mirroring the human-NLP-researcher novelty study's protocol) that collects both novelty/excitement ratings and a separate "predicted long-term fertility" judgment, with a subset of generated ideas tracked for real preprint uptake and citations over 12-18 months.
idea.expected_result: The fertility-reranked pipeline produces idea sets occupying measurably higher-citation-potential regions of idea space and showing more question-level (vs. mere method-level) recombination, while its LLM-judged and human novelty/excitement scores remain statistically indistinguishable from the novelty-optimized baseline — demonstrating that novelty and fertility are separable axes, and that current ideation systems have been optimizing a signal that predicts reviewer excitement but not downstream scientific impact.
idea.grounding: Motivated directly by the finding that AI research agents narrow scientific exploration and drift toward lower-citation regions of the literature despite being tuned for novelty, by the human-study result that retrieval-plus-rerank ideation already beats human experts on blind novelty judgments, by evidence from ML research-agent benchmarking that LLM-judged novelty is poorly correlated with empirical effectiveness, and by the classical science-of-science finding that scientific impact arises from atypical combinations layered on a conventional core — a mechanism this proposal imports into AI ideation evaluation for the first time.

topic: AI systems for generating novel research ideas

idea.title: Execution-Risk-Aware Idea Selection: Closing the Ideation-Execution Gap with Outcome-Supervised Critics
idea.gap: Nearly every current LLM research-ideation system — from prompted generators to literature-grounded pipelines like ResearchAgent and HARPA to diversity-search methods like quality-diversity idea search (e.g. IDEAAgent-style archives) — selects or ranks candidate ideas using generation-time proxies: novelty scores, LLM-judge "excitement" ratings, embedding-distance-from-prior-work, or testability checks performed against the literature alone. But "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study" (Si, Yang, and Hashimoto) found LLM ideas rated more novel than expert ideas yet somewhat less feasible, and the follow-up study "The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas" (Si and Hashimoto) went further: when 43 expert researchers each spent 100+ hours actually executing randomly-assigned LLM-generated versus human-written ideas and the resulting write-ups were blindly reviewed, the LLM ideas' scores dropped sharply relative to their ideation-stage novelty ratings, largely erasing the apparent LLM advantage. This is direct empirical evidence that the very signal essentially every idea-generation system optimizes or filters on — perceived novelty/excitement at ideation time — is decoupled from what actually happens when an idea meets real experimentation. Despite this being demonstrated, no existing system feeds execution-outcome data back into idea generation or selection; the ideation-quality literature and the execution-outcome literature remain separate threads.
idea.proposed_study: (1) Mine a labeled dataset of (idea text, execution-outcome delta, failure-mode tags) by extracting the blind reviewer critiques from the 43 executed projects in the Ideation-Execution Gap study, coding recurring failure modes (e.g., unfair/mismatched baselines, effect sizes within noise, missing ablations, uncontrolled confounds, infeasible scope for the time budget) and pairing them with each idea's ideation-stage novelty/excitement score and its post-execution score. (2) Train or in-context-calibrate an "execution-risk critic" that, given only the pre-execution idea text, predicts the probability and type of these failure modes — explicitly optimized against realized execution-score deltas rather than against novelty or literature-grounded testability. (3) Hold a standard novelty-driven idea generator fixed (e.g., the pipeline used in the original Si et al. study) and produce two matched idea sets of equal size: one reranked/filtered by ideation-time novelty as usual, one reranked/filtered by the execution-risk critic, matching topics across conditions. (4) Run a scaled-down replication of the Ideation-Execution Gap protocol — recruit a smaller panel of domain-expert executors blind to condition, have each implement one assigned idea and write a short paper, then have the write-ups blindly peer-reviewed on the same rubric as the original study.
idea.expected_result: Ideas selected by the execution-risk critic will show a significantly smaller ideation-to-execution score drop than novelty-selected ideas from the same generator, even when their ideation-stage novelty ratings are equal or slightly lower — i.e., execution-outcome-supervised selection predicts realized research value better than novelty-based selection does. This would be the first demonstration that outcome data harvested from actually executing AI-generated ideas can be closed into a training/selection signal for the generator itself, rather than serving only as a post-hoc evaluation of it.
idea.grounding: Directly grounded in Si, Yang, and Hashimoto's "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?" (which established the novelty-feasibility tradeoff in LLM ideation) and Si and Hashimoto's "The Ideation-Execution Gap" (which empirically established that ideation-time novelty judgments fail to predict execution-time outcomes); it also extends testability-driven approaches like HARPA and diversity-search approaches like quality-diversity idea generation, which still rely on proxy signals evaluated without ever touching real execution outcomes. This matters because it targets the central credibility problem of AI-driven scientific discovery — that systems are optimized and marketed on how novel an idea looks rather than on whether it survives contact with actual experimentation — and proposes the first closed feedback loop from execution reality back into idea selection.
